questions.q: A student observes a bivalve (freshwater mussel) and a gastropod (garden snail) and notes both have a shell and a muscular foot. What is the SINGLE most fundamental feature that confirms both belong to Phylum Mollusca, distinct from Arthropoda or Annelida?
questions.a: The presence of a mantle that secretes the shell and forms a mantle cavity housing gills (ctenidia) is the defining synapomorphy of Mollusca. Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton secreted by epidermis (not mantle) and lack a mantle cavity; annelids are segmented with chaetae and lack both shell and mantle. A wrong answer (e.g., "both have a shell") reveals the student confuses analogous structures (shells also in brachiopods, some annelids) with the homologous molluscan mantle-shell complex.

questions.q: In a dissected Pila (apple snail), the mantle cavity lies on the right side of the body and opens to the exterior via a single large opening. In a dissected bivalve (Lamellidens), the mantle cavity is ventral and has two distinct siphons. Explain WHY this difference exists in terms of the animal's mode of life and the torsion event in gastropod evolution.
questions.a: Gastropods undergo torsion (180° twisting of visceral mass) during larval development, bringing the mantle cavity and anus forward over the head; this results in a single posterior opening on the right side. Bivalves are sedentary filter-feeders that burrow; they retain bilateral mantle lobes that fuse ventrally to form inhalant (ventral) and exhalant (dorsal) siphons for water current while buried. A wrong answer (e.g., "bivalves have two openings because they have two shells") shows the student mistakes shell valves for mantle cavity openings and ignores the developmental basis of torsion.

questions.q: A cone snail (Conus) injects venom into a fish using a modified radular tooth. A chiton (Chaetopleura) scrapes algae off rocks with a radula bearing dozens of transverse rows of teeth. Predict the radular formula (arrangement of teeth per row) for each and justify based on feeding mechanism.
questions.a: Cone snail: radula reduced to a single hollow, harpoon-like tooth per row (formula 1+0+1 or similar) — each tooth is a disposable venom-delivery syringe. Chiton: radula with many transverse rows, each row bearing numerous teeth (e.g., 17+1+17 or more) for continuous scraping like a conveyor belt. A wrong answer (e.g., "both have many teeth") reveals the student does not link radular morphology to functional adaptation — venom delivery requires single-shot precision, scraping requires durability and replacement.

questions.q: Compare the circulatory systems of a typical gastropod (Pila) and a cephalopod (Octopus). Identify the key structural difference and explain how it correlates with metabolic rate and locomotion in these two classes.
questions.a: Gastropods have an open circulatory system: heart pumps haemolymph into sinuses (haemocoel) bathing tissues directly; low pressure, slow flow suits slow crawling. Cephalopods have a closed circulatory system: blood confined in vessels (arteries, capillaries, veins) with accessory branchial hearts; high pressure, rapid flow supports active jet propulsion, complex brain, and high metabolic rate. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are open because they are molluscs") shows the student overgeneralises phylum-level traits and misses the cephalopod innovation that enables their predatory lifestyle.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since both earthworms (Annelida) and snails (Mollusca) are coelomate, bilaterally symmetrical, and have a complete digestive system, they should be placed in the same phylum." Evaluate this claim using THREE distinguishing features at the phylum level.
questions.a: The claim is invalid. Three phylum-level distinctions: (1) Body plan — annelids are metamerically segmented (true segmentation with repeated organs); molluscs are unsegmented (except primitive serial repetition in chitons). (2) Exoskeleton — molluscs secrete a calcareous shell via mantle; annelids have a thin collagenous cuticle, no shell. (3) Coelom derivation — annelid coelom is spacious perivisceral cavity; molluscan coelom is reduced to pericardial cavity and gonadal spaces, main body cavity is haemocoel (open circulatory system). A wrong evaluation (e.g., "both are worms") reveals the student relies on superficial habitus rather than fundamental architectural differences.

questions.q: Design a simple field observation to distinguish a living gastropod from a living bivalve without dissecting or removing them from their habitat. List the steps and the decisive observation.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Locate the animal in its microhabitat (snail on vegetation/wall, bivalve buried in mud/sand). (2) Gently touch the anterior end — gastropod extends head with sensory tentacles and eyes; bivalve shows no head, only siphons or valve gaping. (3) Observe locomotion — gastropod glides on a broad flat foot leaving mucus trail; bivalve uses a hatchet-shaped foot for burrowing or byssal threads for attachment. Decisive observation: presence of a distinct head with tentacles and eyes (gastropod) vs. complete absence of head (bivalve). A poor answer (e.g., "look at the shell") fails because shell morphology converges (e.g., limpet looks like a bivalve valve) and some gastropods are shell-less (slugs).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Phylum Mollusca comprises bilaterally symmetrical, ______, coelomate animals with organ-system level of organisation, characterised by a soft unsegmented body typically covered by a calcareous shell, a distinct muscular foot for locomotion, a visceral hump containing most organs, and a mantle that secretes the shell and forms a mantle cavity housing feather-like gills (ctenidia) for respiration and excretion; a unique rasping feeding organ called radula is present in most classes.

Fill in the blank: Pick up a common garden snail (Pila) after monsoon rain — notice its slimy muscular foot gliding on the wet wall, the coiled shell it carries like a portable home, and the two pairs of ______ with eyes at the tips.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can: (1) list the five defining characteristics of Mollusca and explain the function of mantle, mantle cavity, radula, and foot; (2) compare and contrast the four major classes (Gastropoda, Bivalvia, Cephalopoda, Polyplacophora) using a table of shell type, foot modification, radula presence, and habitat; (3) trace the path.
